newsitem.title: FRANCE: LVMH turns up heat on Guinness.
newsitem.headline: LVMH turns up heat on Guinness.

text.p: French luxury goods group LVMH is turning up the heat on one-time ally Guinness Plc by threatening to buy back the British group's participation in their joint distribution ventures, analysts said on Wednesday.

They said LVMH's announcement that it would exercise options to untangle the links between the two companies seemed aimed at forcing Guinness and its merger partner Grand Metropolitan Plc into negotiating with LVMH chairman Bernard Arnault, who opposes the merger.

Arnault, whose group owns 14 percent of Guinness, wanted Guinness to split its brewing and drinks activities and merge the drinks business with LVMH's Moet Hennessy, makers of France's Moet & Chandon champagne and Hennessy cognacs, to create a global drinks leader.

"The ideal solution for Arnault is still to take Moet Hennessy and combine it with the spirits operations of GMG Brands," one analyst said. GMG Brands is the name proposed for the merger between GrandMet and Guinness, known for its renowned stout and makers of leading whisky brands like Johnnie Walker.
But he said he thought the likelihood that Arnault would get his way was small. "The boards of Guinness and Grand Met don't want any more of Arnault's demands. They've purposely marginalised him."
Analysts were unclear how much trouble Arnault could stir up for Guinness, which was his ally in the takeover of LVMH and still owns 34 percent of Moet Hennessy.

LVMH issued a statement on Wednesday saying the Grand Met/Guinness merger constituted a "control event", allowing it to exercise options to buy Guinness's interests in their joint ventures and its 34 percent stake in Moet Hennessy.

"As a result, LVMH will operate the joint ventures independently, with a right to continue to market and distribute on an exclusive basis Guinness brands...in the key markets of China, France, Hong Kong, Japan, Malaysia, Singapore, Taiwan, Thailand and the United States for at least 10 years," the statement said.
"Guinness wanted to develop synergies in this area with Grand Met, with Grand Met products distributed through its ventures and vice versa. That would now seem blocked," said another analyst.
Guinness disputed LVMH's interpretation, suggesting the two companies may end up fighting it out in court.

"Guinness is confident that a 'control event' will not be triggered by the completion of the proposed merger, and that there is therefore no basis for the assertion made by LVMH," it said in a statement.
Paribas Capital Markets analyst Cecile d'Estais said she did not believe LVMH wanted to buy the Guinness stakes in Moet Hennessy and the distribution ventures.
"What they really want to do is merge the wines and spirits businesses and exit Pillsbury, Burger King and the beer business," she said.
With majority control of Moet Hennessy and 14.2 percent of Guinness, LVMH would be the largest shareholder in that business, analysts said.

LVMH said it had proposed a merger of its wines and spirits businesses with those of Guinness. "A similar proposal was made to Guinness and Grand Metropolitan, and this proposal remains open for discussion," it said.
It said that within Guinness and GrandMet, only wines and spirits were clearly complementary.
"LVMH does not believe that shareholder value will be maximised by creating a conglomerate combining certain businesses with no common thread," it said.
LVMH would hold 6.7 percent of GMG Brands.
It has been focussing more on the luxury goods side and recently sold a seven percent stake in Guinness to help pay for the acquisition of San Francisco-based Duty Free Shoppers.

LVMH said that under agreements dating back to 1994, it has an option to buy back Guinness's 34 percent stake in Moet Hennessy at a discount of up to 15 percent. It said the business would be independently valued to determine the price.
Some analysts estimated the price for that stake at around eight billion francs.
